briefs.problem: Technicians lose time and customers get poor service because last-minute cancellations aren't systematically absorbed back into the day's tours.
briefs.solution: A maintenance-visit scheduling tool that assigns technicians to tours and reshuffles the plan when a client cancels.
introduces: a technician-to-visit assignment engine driven by zone/skill/availability rules
a cancellation-triggered rescheduling mechanism (the core new capability)
a dispatcher/planner surface that doesn't exist today
concurrency handling across technicians whose tours can be touched by the same rescheduling event
a notification layer for clients and technicians on schedule changes

challenges.headline: Real-time reoptimization assumed
challenges.premise: The request implies cancellations trigger an immediate reshuffle of the day's tours.
challenges.alternative: A planner-mediated, end-of-day or batch reschedule avoids building a live routing/optimization engine and lets a human absorb ambiguous cases (a technician mid-route, a client who calls back to un-cancel).
challenges.consequence: A synchronous, automatic reoptimization engine is a materially larger build — it needs conflict resolution, rollback on failure, and a UX for a user waiting on a result — than a planner reshuffling a screen once or twice a day.
challenges.recommendation: Settle synchronous-automatic vs. manual-batch rescheduling with the client before estimating; this single choice reshapes the architecture.

challenges.headline: Visit origin left unstated
challenges.premise: Visits are treated as if they simply exist, ready to be scheduled.
challenges.alternative: If visits are generated from a recurring maintenance contract (a fixed frequency per client), the real system boundary includes contract/schedule generation upstream, not just tour assignment.
challenges.consequence: Scoping this as 'just a routing tool' risks a significant miss if a contract-driven visit generator turns out to be in scope.
challenges.recommendation: Confirm with the client whether visits come from a recurring contract or are entered ad hoc before sizing the build.

challenges.headline: "Last moment" left unquantified
challenges.premise: The request names a last-minute cancellation trigger without defining when 'last minute' starts.
challenges.alternative: A stated cutoff (e.g., cancellations inside 4 hours of the visit vs. the day before) lets the team design distinct, appropriate handling for each case instead of one catch-all path.
challenges.consequence: Without a threshold, error handling and technician/client UX can't be designed consistently, and the team risks building for the wrong urgency level.
challenges.recommendation: Ask the client to quantify the cancellation window and tie it explicitly to the rescheduling behavior.

complexity_reasons: undecided synchronous vs. batch rescheduling model
possible need for a route/assignment optimization algorithm
concurrency across technicians and same-day reassignments
unclear whether visits originate from a recurring contract, which would widen scope
briefs.cost_driver: the rescheduling engine and whether it must reoptimize tours in real time
risks: Over-building a full optimization/routing engine when a simpler planner-driven reassignment screen would meet the actual need.
No visibility into today's process (paper, spreadsheet, another tool) makes it hard to size migration effort or validate assumptions with users.
Same-day, multi-technician reassignment is a natural concurrency hazard: two cancellations processed near-simultaneously can double-book or drop a slot if not designed for.
Notification expectations (channel, timing, recipients) are undefined and easy to underestimate once client and technician-facing needs are compared.
If visits turn out to be contract-generated, the true scope extends well beyond tour planning.

opportunities.text: Build the assignment engine (zone/skill/availability rules) as a configurable rule set rather than hardcoded logic, so rules can vary by client or region later.
Design the schedule-change notification path as a shared mechanism (client-facing and technician-facing) rather than two one-off implementations.

If a real-time reoptimization engine is ultimately required, structure it so it could later serve other dispatch scenarios (urgent insert, multi-day rebalancing) rather than only cancellation-driven reshuffles.

next_steps: Confirm whether visits originate from a recurring maintenance contract or are entered ad hoc — this changes the system boundary.
Settle whether rescheduling must be real-time/automatic or can be planner-mediated and batched.
Quantify the 'last moment' cancellation threshold and define who is authorized to trigger a reassignment.
Map the current process (even informally) to validate assumptions and estimate migration effort.

decisions.decision: The visit lifecycle will include at minimum: planned → completed/cancelled → rescheduled.
A dispatcher/planner role will exist in the system, even though the request never names one.
decisions.why: Someone has to own reassignment decisions when automation can't confidently resolve a conflict (e.g., no available technician in zone).
decisions.alternative: A fully automatic system with no human oversight.
decisions.tradeoff: Extra role and admin surface to build, in exchange for a safety net on exception cases that a pure algorithm would mishandle.

decisions.decision: Any schedule change will trigger a notification to the affected client and/or technician.

briefs.problem: Technician maintenance visits are scheduled with no defined way to reassign work when a client cancels late, risking wasted technician time and missed intervention windows.
briefs.solution: A tour-planning tool that organizes technician visits into daily routes and dynamically reorganizes them when a client cancels at the last minute.
introduces: a technician-to-client assignment engine driven by skill, zone and availability
a rescheduling workflow triggered by last-minute cancellations
a planner/dispatcher role and its permissions surface
a notification layer to keep technicians and clients in sync with schedule changes
possibly a recurring-visit generation engine if maintenance is contract-driven

challenges.headline: Unknown origin of visits
challenges.premise: The request assumes visits simply exist to be organized into tours, without saying whether they come from a recurring maintenance contract or are created ad hoc.
challenges.alternative: If visits are generated from recurring contracts (frequency per equipment/site), the system needs a generation engine upstream of any tour planning; if they're created case by case, the scope is just scheduling and reassignment logic.
challenges.consequence: Building the tour/reassignment logic before settling this risks a rework of the data model and workflow once the real visit source is known.
challenges.recommendation: Confirm with the client whether visits originate from maintenance contracts or ad hoc requests before scoping the workflow.

challenges.headline: Automatic vs validated reassignment
challenges.premise: The request implies the system reorganizes the tour itself when a client cancels, without saying whether this is automatic or reviewed by a human.
challenges.alternative: A first version where the system proposes a reassignment and a planner validates it avoids betting the whole build on an optimization engine that has to get skill/zone/availability rules right on day one.
challenges.consequence: Full automation without proven business rules risks sending the wrong technician (skill or SLA mismatch) with no human checkpoint to catch it.
challenges.recommendation: Confirm whether a dispatcher exists and should approve reassignments, or whether the client truly wants a hands-off optimization engine from the start.

challenges.headline: No stated assignment rules
challenges.premise: The request treats technician-client matching as a given, but nothing defines how competence, zone or availability actually constrain who can be assigned where.
challenges.alternative: Capturing these constraints as explicit, possibly per-contract-type rules turns 'reassign the visit' from a vague dispatch decision into a checkable, testable rule set.
challenges.consequence: Without these rules made explicit, any 'automatic reassignment' is really an unverifiable black box that can silently violate SLAs or send an unqualified technician.
challenges.recommendation: Document assignment rules (skill, zone, availability, contract-specific variations) before estimating the engine.

complexity_reasons: assignment engine with skill/zone/availability constraints, not yet defined
concurrent last-minute reassignments the same day (race conditions on tour slots)
workflow shape depends entirely on an unanswered question (recurring vs ad hoc visits)
notification and permission layers currently unspecified but operationally essential
briefs.cost_driver: the technician-to-client assignment and rescheduling engine, whose rules are entirely undefined today
risks: No current-process baseline makes it hard to size the gap or estimate effort accurately.
Automatic reassignment without documented business rules could send an unqualified or out-of-zone technician.
Multiple same-day cancellations reassigned concurrently across technicians can produce conflicting or duplicate tour changes.
No permission model defined yet for who can edit a tour or validate a reschedule — likely to surface late, at acceptance testing.
Rescheduling without reliable notification to technician and client loses most of its operational value.

opportunities.text: Build the technician-assignment logic (skill, zone, availability) as a standalone rule engine rather than hardcoded logic, so future rule changes (per contract or region) don't require redevelopment.
Design the notification layer generically (event → role → channel) so it can serve any future schedule-change event, not just cancellations.
If visits turn out to be contract-driven, build the visit-generation engine as a separate, reusable component decoupled from the tour/reassignment logic.

next_steps: Confirm whether maintenance visits come from a recurring contract or are created ad hoc — this determines whether a generation engine is in scope.
Clarify whether rescheduling after a cancellation should be automatic or validated by a human planner.
Document today's assignment rules (skill, zone, availability) and how they vary by contract or site.
Map the current planning process and who is allowed to edit a tour or approve a reschedule.

decisions.decision: The tour (one route per technician) is the core planning unit.
A last-minute client cancellation triggers a rescheduling event rather than leaving the slot simply empty.
decisions.why: The request explicitly names cancellation-driven replanning as the scenario to handle.
decisions.alternative: Leaving cancelled slots unfilled and handled manually by the technician or planner.
decisions.tradeoff: Building a rescheduling workflow adds engineering effort in exchange for better technician utilization.

briefs.solution: A maintenance-visit scheduling system organized by technician tours, with a rescheduling mechanism triggered when a client cancels.
introduces: a tour/route construction engine that assigns visits to technicians and sequences them
a rescheduling/re-optimization engine reacting to cancellation events
a dispatcher/planner role and admin surface that doesn't currently exist in the described request
a notification capability toward clients and/or technicians
a waitlist or standby mechanism for filling freed slots
concurrency handling across technicians and tours during reassignment

challenges.headline: Origin of visits left undefined
challenges.premise: The request treats visits as ready-made units to slot into a tour and reshuffle on cancellation.
challenges.alternative: If visits actually come from a recurring maintenance contract, the system first needs to generate them periodically and automatically — a materially bigger build than a reactive rescheduling tool bolted onto a manual planning process.
challenges.consequence: Sizing the project without settling this risks discovering mid-build that the real scope is 'generate and maintain the entire visit pipeline', not just 'reschedule when cancelled'.
challenges.recommendation: Confirm with the client whether visits originate from a recurring contract, ad hoc requests, or manual entry before any estimate is given.

challenges.headline: Automatic reassignment assumed
challenges.premise: Rescheduling is framed as something the system does when a cancellation happens, with no mention of who controls it.
challenges.alternative: A dispatcher who reviews and validates each reassignment before it's applied is a different build than a fully autonomous re-optimization algorithm — it needs a review/override UI, not just a scoring engine.
challenges.consequence: Building a fully autonomous engine when the client actually wants human oversight over-invests in algorithmic sophistication and under-builds the validation workflow the planner actually needs.
challenges.recommendation: Clarify whether a planner/dispatcher role exists and whether rescheduling decisions require their approval.

challenges.headline: No-fill scenario unaddressed
challenges.premise: The request implies a freed slot after a cancellation gets absorbed somehow, without saying what happens when nothing can fill it.
challenges.alternative: Explicitly defining the fallback — a visible gap in the technician's day, a waitlist offer, or a shift to the next day — turns the central edge case of this feature into a designed behavior instead of a surprise found in testing.
challenges.consequence: Leaving this open risks technicians ending up with the exact unproductive gaps the tool was commissioned to eliminate.
challenges.recommendation: Define the no-fill fallback behavior before designing the rescheduling logic.

complexity_reasons: real-time re-optimization logic triggered by cancellations
unresolved visit-origin question could double the scope (generation engine vs. rescheduling-only tool)
concurrency across technicians and tours when reassigning slots
assignment rules (zone, skill, client-specific) not yet defined but will shape the whole tour-building logic
briefs.cost_driver: the rescheduling/re-optimization engine and the assignment rules it depends on
risks: Visit origin (recurring contract vs. ad hoc vs. manual) is unknown — could turn this from a rescheduling tool into a full visit-generation system.
No documented current process — hard to validate that the new system is actually an improvement without a baseline.
Concurrent cancellations/reassignments across technicians create race conditions if not designed for from the start.
Permission model is undefined — adding a dispatcher approval step late would touch the core workflow already built.
No success metrics defined — acceptance testing has nothing concrete to measure against.

opportunities.text: Design the rescheduling engine as a general re-optimization service (not cancellation-only) so it can also absorb technician absence or emergency visit insertion.
A waitlist/standby mechanism built for cancellations could later serve as a general demand-buffer whenever capacity is constrained.

next_steps: Confirm whether visits originate from a recurring contract, ad hoc requests, or manual entry — this determines the real project size.
Clarify whether a dispatcher/planner role exists and whether they must approve reassignments, or whether rescheduling is fully automatic.
Define the fallback behavior when no replacement can absorb a cancelled slot.
Agree on success metrics (fill rate, rescheduling delay, technician idle time) to anchor acceptance criteria.

decisions.decision: Core actors are at minimum Technician and Client, with a dispatcher/planner role assumed necessary even though not explicitly named in the request
Visit lifecycle assumed to include at least planned → completed/cancelled → rescheduled

open_decisions: Current scheduling process (Excel, paper, another tool, none) and why it fails today
Success criteria for the new system (fill rate, rescheduling speed, client satisfaction)
Assignment rules between technician and client (zone, skill, contract-specific)
Who can plan, cancel, and reschedule a tour (permissions)
Notification scope: who is told (client, technician, both) and through which channel
Whether tour/assignment rules vary by client, region or contract (configurability)
Constraints: delays, geographic zones, regulatory or contractual limits
Reporting/audit needs on rescheduling history
Acceptance scenarios and rollout plan
